name: Colin Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the island, on the one crew that keeps the power on for about nine thousand people. Mostly we're replacing old wooden poles with stronger ones and moving lines away from the cliff edge, because the winter storms keep getting worse. I'm the junior, so I'm on the ground running the auger, guiding the new pole in with a tag line, and cleaning up afterwards. We meet at the yard by the harbour at seven, and on a clear day you can see the mainland. I love being outdoors and I love a problem; what wears me out is being the slow one on a crew of people half my age.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty years as an engineer on fishing boats, keeping old diesels alive in a gale. The fleet shrank to almost nothing after the quota cuts, and in 2023 my skipper sold up. Fishing pay goes up and down, and we'd put most of what we had into getting our two through college, so there wasn't much of a cushion. I use AI for everything now: I had it teach me the line theory, I photograph a pole tag and ask it what I'm looking at. The lads call me the professor, and not entirely kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest. At work I'd say, well, I'll keep using it anyway, it's still the best tutor I ever had. Online I'd probably post something about how the useful bits were real even if the big promises weren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes much for me. The poles still rot, the storms still come, and I'd still be learning. I'd just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the apprenticeship and keep using AI to study for my next level. I'd try to save something each month, say fifty, toward a proper cushion, which we've never had. I'd maybe start doing small diesel repair jobs for the harbour boats on my week off, because there's still a few left and they pay cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little let down. I like new things, so a quiet future is a bit of a shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the lads call you the professor not entirely kindly. What's that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it bothers some of them that the oldest bloke on the crew is the one with his phone out asking it questions. Then again, last month Jamie couldn't work out a sag table and came and asked me quietly at lunch. So it cuts both ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Diesel jobs on your week off. Is that realistic, with your knees and your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably one job a fortnight, not more. Grace would say I'm doing too much, and she'd be right. But fifty here and a hundred there is how we'll get a cushion, because the wage on its own won't do it.

S0.say: He's a bit disappointed, but would keep using AI as the best tutor he ever had. Online he'd say the useful parts were real even if the big promises weren't.
S0.think: Nothing changes much for him: poles still rot, storms still come and he's still learning. He would just carry on.
S0.do: Keeps going with his apprenticeship and keeps studying with AI. Tries to save fifty a month and takes on small diesel repair jobs for harbour boats on his weeks off, about one a fortnight.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly let down, because he enjoys new things.
S0.quote: I think it bothers some of them that the oldest bloke on the crew is the one with his phone out asking it questions.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is an enthusiastic adopter who uses AI daily as a tutor and is slightly let down by a quiet future. His thin savings come from irregular fishing pay and helping his children through college. He is already thinking about small side income from his old marine trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news if we're sensible about it. At work I'd tell the lads to get comfortable with the tools now. Online I'd say the companies and the government both need to help people make the switch, not just one or the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it suits me. I'm slow on the pole but quick with the tech, and if the crew starts using drones for inspections and AI for storm planning, I'm the one who'll pick that up first. The island will still need people on the ground for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to put me on any new kit trials in the first few months, drones especially. I'd do the drone licence on my own time if they wouldn't pay. I'd keep the diesel jobs going on the side, because more income is never a bad idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I'd feel like the change was coming my way for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's coming your way for once. When wasn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the fleet shrank. The quota cuts came from far away, and there was nothing to learn, nothing to switch to, the fish just weren't ours anymore. This would be the first change in my working life where being curious actually helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the drone licence cost, and where would that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've read it's about fifteen hundred with the course and the test. I'd pay it off over a few months from the diesel jobs, and Grace would raise an eyebrow. But if it gets me onto the inspection side, it pays for itself in a year.

S1.say: This is good news if people are sensible about it. He would tell the lads to get comfortable with the tools and say companies and government both need to help people switch.
S1.think: He thinks it suits him, being slow on the pole but quick with technology. The island will still need ground crews for years.
S1.do: Asks to join new equipment trials, especially drones, and pays for a drone licence himself if needed, about fifteen hundred over a few months. Keeps doing diesel repair jobs on the side.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, feeling the change is coming his way for once.
S1.quote: This would be the first change in my working life where being curious actually helps.
S1.fieldNote: For Colin, steady disruption is a chance rather than a threat, in contrast to the fishing collapse he couldn't adapt to. He is ready to spend scarce money on a drone licence because he sees a clear payoff. His view on who should help is balanced between companies and government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough, and we need the government and the companies to move fast together. At work I'd try to keep people calm and practical. Online I'd share anything useful about where the new work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty, with no savings to speak of. Even with my tech habits, if a robot can replace a pole and an AI can plan the storm response, there may not be a place for me on the island. I'd hope there's still a job looking after the robots, but I wouldn't bet the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to the company and ask to be trained on the robots as they come in, maintenance and repair, which is what I did with diesels for thirty years. I'd look for that kind of work on the mainland too, even if it meant moving. And we'd cut back hard at home, no trips, no new anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My stomach drops, but I still feel like I'd find a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to the mainland. What would that mean for Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd hate it. Her mother's on the island, and her job at the ferry office is the only one she's ever had. If I had to, I'd go over during the week and come back at weekends, like the fishing days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the two years give you, compared to the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much time, but enough to get to the front of the queue. I've watched people wait too long before, with the boats. If I'm first to learn the robots, I might be the one they keep.

S2.say: It's going to be rough, and government and companies need to move fast together. He would try to keep colleagues calm and share information on new work.
S2.think: At sixty with no savings, even his tech habits might not save his place on the island if robots replace poles and AI plans storm response. He hopes for robot maintenance work but wouldn't bet on it.
S2.do: Asks straight away to be trained on robot maintenance and repair, and looks for that work on the mainland, commuting weekly if needed. Cuts back hard at home.
S2.feel: Anxious, with his stomach dropping, but still feeling he'd find a way.
S2.quote: I'd hope there's still a job looking after the robots, but I wouldn't bet the house on it.
S2.fieldNote: Colin's adaptability keeps him from despair even in the fastest scenario, but thin savings make it a real worry. He draws on his thirty years keeping engines running as a bridge to robot maintenance. Moving would cost his wife a great deal, and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start today. At work I'd push for training on the new kit. Online I'd post about how people can get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. That's enough time to make myself the robot man on the island, the one who fixes them when the salt air gets into them, which it will. I think I'd be fine, if I start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone licence in the first year and any robotics maintenance course the company or college offers. I'd keep the diesel side jobs going and put that money in savings. I'd also look into setting up a small repair business for robots and drones on the island, for when they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly I'd be busy. Busy is good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A repair business for robots. How serious are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half serious. Salt and wind wreck machines here; I spent thirty years proving that on boat engines. If the company brings in robots and the nearest repair shop is on the mainland, someone on the island will make a living fixing them, and I'd like it to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mainly. Five years isn't long to build a cushion, and if the business idea fails, I've got nothing. Grace would say, Colin, you're sixty-three, not thirty, and she'd have a point.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start today. He would push for training on new equipment and post about getting ready.
S3.think: At sixty-three he could make himself the island's robot repairer, fixing machines damaged by salt air. He thinks he'd be fine if he starts now.
S3.do: Gets his drone licence in the first year and takes any robotics maintenance course on offer. Saves his diesel side income and looks into a small island repair business for robots and drones.
S3.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly busy, which suits him.
S3.quote: Salt and wind wreck machines here; I spent thirty years proving that on boat engines.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Colin turn his marine engineering past into a plan to repair robots on the island. He is honest that the money is thin and the idea could fail. His wife's reminder about his age keeps the plan grounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up, so let's use it. At work I'd tell the lads to start learning now, not in year nine. Online I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so I'd likely be retired or working part-time by then. For me it's a chance to get properly set up first. I'd probably enjoy watching it arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship, do the drone and robotics courses, and build the side business slowly. I'd save steadily, maybe a hundred a month. I'd talk to my son, who works in an office on the mainland, about what he's going to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd feel like I had time to get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the tools early, like I did, and to have a second skill in his hands. He works in logistics planning, which is exactly what AI eats first. He'd probably already have a plan, to be fair; he's more organised than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been upbeat throughout. Is there anything you're not saying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm tired, some days. My body is fifty-eight even if my head isn't. If I'm honest, the thing I worry about isn't the robots, it's whether my knees last long enough to see them.

S4.say: Ten years is a decent run-up, so let's use it. He would tell younger crewmates to start learning now, not in year nine.
S4.think: At sixty-eight he would likely be retired or part-time. He sees the decade as a chance to get properly set up and would probably enjoy watching AGI arrive.
S4.do: Finishes his apprenticeship, takes drone and robotics courses and builds a side business slowly. Saves around a hundred a month and talks to his son about his office job's future.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, feeling he has time to get it right.
S4.quote: The thing I worry about isn't the robots, it's whether my knees last long enough to see them.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Colin is genuinely calm and even looking forward to the change. When pressed he admits physical tiredness, which is his real worry. His concern for his son reflects his sense that office planning work is more exposed than his own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to save and no time to learn. What would help is free training for older workers on the new machines, and some kind of bridge to pension for people my age if the training doesn't work out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the islands, and places like them. When the ferry stops, we're on our own, and if the power's down the robots won't be coming over to fix it. Out here, the one who knows how to fix things is the one who keeps the lights on.

headlineQuote: Out here, the one who knows how to fix things is the one who keeps the lights on.
portrait: Colin Usman is a 58-year-old junior lineworker on an island crew replacing old poles and moving lines away from the cliffs, after thirty years as a fishing boat engineer. He and his wife Grace, who works at the ferry office, have little saved after irregular fishing pay and putting their two children through college. He uses AI every day as a tutor and sees steady change as finally coming his way. Even in the 2028 picture he looks for robot maintenance work, though thin savings make him anxious and moving would be hard on Grace. With more time he plans drone and robotics courses and a small island repair business.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because there would be no time to save or to learn.
whatWouldHelp: Free training for older workers on the new machines, plus a bridge to pension if the training doesn't work out.
